ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Discoid Lupus Erythematosus is a chronic skin disease with disc‑shaped plaques that scar. It is a form of cutaneous lupus, often limited to skin but can precede systemic disease.

sections.p: DLE presents as erythematous, scaly plaques with a characteristic discoid shape. Diagnosis is clinical plus histology showing interface dermatitis, follicular plugging, and mucin deposition. ANA may be negative.
b: Look for scarring, alopecia, and photosensitivity.

t.b: Confirms interface dermatitis and follicular plugging; a positive result supports DLE.
Usually negative; a positive ANA suggests systemic lupus.
Helps differentiate from seborrheic dermatitis; a central white scar with peripheral erythema is typical.

sections.p: The SLEDAI‑2K skin score is used; mild (1–4), moderate (5–9), severe (>10). Staging guides treatment intensity.
b: Severe: extensive plaques, significant scarring, possible systemic involvement.

sections.p: The exact trigger is unknown; UV light, infections, and hormonal changes are common. In low‑resource settings, infections like HIV and TB may exacerbate.
Patients report red, scaly patches that itch or burn. Plaques are often on sun‑exposed areas, especially the scalp, face, and ears. Scarring alopecia is common.
Tests confirm diagnosis and rule out systemic disease. Use available resources wisely.

t.b: Low levels may indicate systemic disease.

sections.p: Complications include irreversible scarring, secondary infection, and rare progression to systemic lupus. Watch for rapid ulceration or new systemic symptoms.
Treat the skin and prevent progression. First line is sun protection and topical steroids. Systemic therapy is reserved for severe or refractory cases.

t.b: Chosen for local effect, minimal systemic absorption.
Preferred for long‑term use; monitor for retinal toxicity.
Used short course; avoid long‑term due to side effects.

sections.p: Regular skin checks, sun‑exposure counseling, and monitoring for systemic signs are essential. Educate patients on early signs of systemic disease.
b: Annual ANA and complement checks if systemic signs appear

sections.p: Differential includes seborrheic dermatitis, psoriasis, tinea corporis, and sarcoidosis.
b: Tinea corporis – ring‑like border, central clearing

sections.p: ANA can be negative in DLE, leading to under‑diagnosis of systemic disease. Skin biopsy may miss early lesions.
b: Biopsy of a healed plaque may show only scarring

faq.a: Yes, about 10–20% of patients may develop systemic lupus over time.

faq.q: Is sun protection enough to prevent flares?
faq.a: Sun protection reduces flares but does not cure DLE; topical therapy is still needed.
Antibiotics are not effective unless there is a secondary bacterial infection.

exam: Explain the diagnostic criteria for discoid lupus erythematosus and how they differ from systemic lupus erythematosus.
Describe the first‑line topical treatment for DLE and justify its use.
Discuss red flags that would prompt referral to a rheumatologist.
